stories.title: Agentic AI Startup Uniti Draws More Clients Amid $12M Series A
stories.excerpt: Uniti, an agentic artificial intelligence platform for real estate property managers, is experiencing rapid growth in client demand and funding as proptech companies compete to solve large operators’ everyday workflow challenges. Founded in February 2024, the Manhattan-based startup has seen demand for its agentic AI services grow across real estate asset classes, including with customers such as Regus, StorQuest, RHP Properties, Storage King USA and others. The company’s agentic AI layer can run leasing, maintenance, collections, reviews and renewals across voice, email, SMS and chat for operators in self-storage, manufactured housing, multifamily, senior living and flexible workspace. The company is delivering measurable operational and commercial results, including 214 percent return on investment for one enterprise self-storage operator, according to Uniti. In addition, 94 percent of its pilots converted into long-term customer contracts, with 306 percent net revenue retention as customers expand across additional properties and workflows. “Commercial real estate runs a trillion dollars of operational labor per year,” said Francesco Decamilli, co-founder and CEO of Uniti. “The way we see it, it’s the same job repeated millions of times, geography by geography, property by property, asset class by asset class. There’s always someone who’s calling about who needs to pay a bill, who needs to file a maintenance request. Property teams work 9 to 5 and customers show up 24/7. For the first time, AI agents are genuinely good enough not to just answer, but to complete workflows end to end, even to transact. They can do the work itself — taking a payment, signing a lease or resolving a maintenance ticket. “So what we’re setting out to build is a unique agentic layer for real estate that works across the entire cycle of the tenant experience.” The Uniti platform integrates with 15 property management systems and uses large language models to locali
bullets: Uniti AI (Manhattan) raised $12M Series A; serves Regus, StorQuest, RHP Properties across multifamily, self-storage, senior living.
Agentic AI platform automates leasing, maintenance, collections, renewals via voice, email, SMS; 94% pilot conversion rate.
306% net revenue retention as customers expand; one self-storage operator reported 214% ROI.
stories.summary: Uniti, a Manhattan-based agentic AI startup founded February 2024, closed a Series A and is expanding rapidly across multifamily, self-storage, senior living, and flexible workspace operators. The platform automates leasing, maintenance, collections, and renewals across multiple channels. Customers show exceptional retention (306% NRR) and ROI (214% for one self-storage operator), with 94% of pilots converting to long-term contracts.
stories.impact: Proptech automation that reduces labor intensity and improves operational margins will intensify competitive pressure on operators lacking AI-driven workflows. Multifamily operators who adopt early gain cost and efficiency advantages; those who lag risk becoming less competitive on rents and asset quality. This signals accelerating technology adoption across institutional and mid-market operators.

stories.title: Jeff Rosenfeld of North River Partners: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which was enacted earlier this month, promises to greatly impact U.S. real estate when it goes into effect in January. The U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate passed the legislation — without President Donald Trump’s signature — with the intention of boosting housing supply and cutting construction red tape. The heavily bipartisan legislation also promises to greatly restrict large institutional investors by banning them from competing with traditional buyers for existing single-family homes. But there’s some loopholes that companies can exploit to get around the ban, according to Jeff Rosenfeld, managing partner and co-founder of New York City-based real estate credit platform North River Partners. As a lender focused on residential construction across the U.S., North River is experiencing the effects of the bill on developers and owners firsthand, Rosenfeld said. North River has also been doing some deals of its own lately. In April, the firm, along with Amzak Capital Partners, provided $68.5 million of total financing to CedarSt Companies for Flagler Gateway, a 215-unit multifamily development in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., where Rosenfeld said the firm sees a “really exciting housing market for decades to come.” Commercial Observer sat down with Rosenfeld last week to discuss the ROAD to Housing Act and how it might impact housing investment trends, as well as how the Federal Reserve’s vote on benchmark interest rates might go on Wednesday. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. bullets: 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (enacted January 2025) bans large institutional investors from competing for single-family homes.
Bill promises red-tape reduction and increased housing supply; North River Partners (NYC-based lender) sees firsthand developer impact.
North River closed $68.5M financing (with Amzak Capital) for CedarSt's Flagler Gateway multifamily in April.
stories.summary: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which took effect in January 2025, restricts institutional investors from purchasing existing single-family homes to boost housing supply and reduce regulatory burden. However, loopholes exist that sophisticated investors can exploit. North River Partners, a residential construction lender, is observing the bill's impact on developers and has been active in deal-making, including a $68.5M co-investment in Flagler Gateway multifamily.
stories.impact: Single-family investor ban redirects institutional capital toward multifamily development and creates relative scarcity in single-family acquisitions, potentially strengthening multifamily rents and development feasibility in markets where institutional SFR presence was high. Regulatory tailwinds on entitlements and supply could accelerate starts, but market absorption and capital competition will intensify. Watch for deal flow acceleration in Q1–Q2 2025 as lenders and developers move ahead of any further regulatory tightening.

stories.title: Gotham Organization’s Matthew, Nicole and Ben Picket On the Family Firm’s Next Moves
stories.excerpt: The Picket family has been running the Gotham Organization, an owner, developer, operator and investment manager, since 1912, and has only ever handed over the reins to the next generation — never an outsider. The New York City-based (and -focused) firm was founded by Nathan Picket, great-grandfather of current CEO David Picket, who says Gotham is run under the mantra “Do good to do well.” “It’s something we live by,” David Picket said. “We’re not in this for short-term gain. We’re in this for the long haul. It’s been 114 years. That we’ve made it this far — five generations — what are the odds? It’s about taking a long-term view and about being fair with your lenders and partners, and treating your tenants with respect.” That’s five generations and counting at Gotham. Picket’s three children — Matthew Picket (35), Nicole Picket (32) and Ben Picket (30) — each work in the family business, with Matthew and Nicole recently taking on more senior leadership roles. Ben is currently working toward his MBA at Columbia University, but all of the Pickets got their undergraduate degrees at Cornell. The Picket children were raised with the principle that education and intelligence are valuable tools, and they say they bring that to their work at Gotham. Matthew Picket is a principal at Gotham, where he is focused on driving the firm’s development pipeline, while expanding into new markets, like South Florida. Nicole Picket is also a principal, and spends her days overseeing the refinancings, recapitalizations and dispositions of Gotham’s existing assets, in addition to finding new opportunities to grow the firm’s portfolio through multifamily acquisitions. Nicole helped build the firm’s 2024 acquisition of the Aire, a luxury rental property at 200 West 67th Street, in a $265 million joint venture with Carlyle Group. bullets: Gotham Organization (NYC): five-generation family firm (1912–2025) now transitioning leadership to Matthew, Nicole, and Ben Picket.
CEO David Picket: long-term hold strategy, fair treatment of lenders/partners/tenants; no outsider management in 114 years.
Matthew (35), Nicole (32), and Ben (30) taking expanded roles; company remains NYC-focused owner-developer-operator-manager.
stories.summary: Gotham Organization, a New York City–based owner-developer-operator and investment manager founded in 1912, is now in its fifth generation with Matthew, Nicole, and Ben Picket stepping into expanded leadership roles under patriarch David Picket. The firm has never hired an outside CEO and operates under a long-term, relationship-focused philosophy. Gotham remains NYC-focused and continues selective multifamily development.
stories.impact: Limited direct market impact; primarily a leadership succession story. Gotham's long-term, relationship-driven approach and NYC footprint make it a stable, patient capital source and operator. Generational transitions in family offices typically result in modest portfolio rebalancing or expansion over 2–3 years; monitor for any shift in appetite for development risk or asset class mix.

stories.title: AI Company Antares Labs Launches With $7M Seed Round
stories.excerpt: Chicago-based Antares Labs, a builder of custom artificial intelligence solutions for real estate operations, is announcing its launch with a $7.25 million seed round, Commercial Observer has learned. Proptech venture capital firm Fifth Wall led the round, alongside an investor list of Base10 Partners, Bloomberg Beta and Sandwith Ventures. Noaman Ahmad, Antares Labs’ co-founder and CEO, previously served as chief financial officer at proptech company Doma and tech consultancy firm Keystone. Ahmad told Commercial Observer that he observed a gap between the real estate industry’s rich data and its uptake of technologies that could help them make the fullest use of it. “Most of these companies have now realized that they need to do something using the power of AI, because if they don’t, they’re going to lose the competitive edge over the next year or two years,” Ahmad said. Antares Labs’ tailor-made AI systems digest and build upon clients’ institutional knowledge, proprietary data and workflows. Antares’ current client, real estate developer and investment manager Quarterra, is using these services to identify and target new submarkets and land parcels, Ahmad said. “We’re coming to market with a very different angle on this,” Ahmad said. “We’re not bringing a tool. We’re not building an agent for them. We’re talking to them about how they think about AI broadly across their enterprise.” Other use cases of Antares Labs’ consultancy model include shrinking the time between tenant departures and arrivals for a shopping center-focused real estate investment trust, and discovering current and future inventory insights for an industrial landlord. Antares Labs’ platforms are built to be model-agnostic, meaning that a client can take their pick of providers like OpenAI or Gemini, and easily adjust according to needs or cost pressures. bullets: Antares Labs (Chicago) raised $7.25M seed round led by Fifth Wall; Base10, Bloomberg Beta, Sandwith co-invested.

stories.summary: Chicago-based Antares Labs, founded by ex-Doma CFO Noaman Ahmad, launched with a $7.25M seed round led by proptech VC Fifth Wall to build custom AI solutions that help real estate operators leverage proprietary data and institutional workflows. Antares digests client data to improve decision-making; current client Quarterra is using it for submarket targeting and opportunity identification.
stories.impact: Another signal of proptech capital chasing operational and capital-allocation efficiency gains. Custom AI that improves site selection and financial underwriting could reduce real estate operators' time-to-decision and improve deal quality, but creates a widening advantage for firms that invest in AI literacy and integration. For developers, this suggests sophistication in competitor underwriting is rising; expect tighter margins on markets/assets where data-driven competitors are active.

stories.title: Affiliated Closes Financing on Mixed-Income Fort Lauderdale Apartment Venture
stories.excerpt: Affiliated Development has closed on a $74 million construction loan with Pacific Life Insurance Company for The Cove, a mixed-use, mixed-income multifamily development on the northwest corner of Sunrise Boulevard and Federal Highway in Fort Lauderdale. Just over half of the 374 units will be restricted to families earning 120% of the Area Median Income. In exchange for the rent restrictions, Fort Lauderdale and Broward County offered tax rebates. The Cove will rise on the site of a former hotel property. The site was home to the Clarion Inn and The Link hotel until it was recently demolished. Moss Construction is serving as general contractor on The Cove. Rinka is the project’s architect. The project is being capitalized with a $74 million construction loan from Pacific Life Insurance Company, equity from Affiliated Housing Impact Fund, LP and family office capital partners. Construction on The Cove is expected to commence immediately following closing. The post Affiliated Closes Financing on Mixed-Income Fort Lauderdale Apartment Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Affiliated Development closed $74M construction loan (Pacific Life) for The Cove, Fort Lauderdale mixed-income multifamily; 374 units.
~187 units (>50%) restricted to 120% AMI; Fort Lauderdale & Broward County offered tax rebates for affordability.
Site: former Clarion Inn & Link hotel (demolished); Moss Construction, Rinka Architect; construction starts immediately.
stories.summary: Affiliated Development secured a $74M construction loan from Pacific Life Insurance Company for The Cove, a 374-unit mixed-income multifamily development in Fort Lauderdale on the site of two demolished hotels. Over half the units are restricted to families earning 120% AMI; the developer received tax incentives from Fort Lauderdale and Broward County in exchange. Construction is commencing immediately.
stories.impact: Demonstrates continued lender appetite for mixed-income multifamily in South Florida high-growth submarket. Tax incentives and density entitlements on former hotel sites signal municipal push to convert underutilized hospitality assets into rental housing—a supply creation opportunity. Fort Lauderdale's willingness to rebate taxes for workforce housing suggests demand for middle-income rental supply; watch for similar redevelopment pipelines at distressed hotel properties in similar Sunbelt markets (Tampa, Phoenix, Austin).

stories.title: Olmstead Signs Luckin Coffee to 10-Year Lease in Hudson Square
stories.excerpt: Olmstead Properties has signed Luckin Coffee to a new 10-year, 1,200-square-foot retail lease at 180 Varick St., bringing one of the country’s fastest-growing coffee brands to the base of the historic Hudson Square office building. Luckin Coffee will replace a neighborhood pizzeria and deli that had occupied the storefront for more than 40 years before its longtime owner retired. Steven Marvin of Olmstead Properties represented ownership. “Luckin Coffee is an outstanding addition to 180 Varick St. and exactly the type of tenant we were seeking for the building,” said Marvin.  “As Hudson Square continues to evolve as one of Manhattan’s most dynamic office neighborhoods, we’re focused on bringing in amenities that enhance the daily experience for our tenants while serving the surrounding community. Luckin has built a strong following by delivering a modern, convenient coffee experience, and we’re excited to welcome them to the building.” 180 Varick St. has been owned by the Rosenblatt family since it was developed in the 1920s by Sam Rosenblatt’s great-grandfather, making it Olmstead Properties’ longest-held asset. The post Olmstead Signs Luckin Coffee to 10-Year Lease in Hudson Square appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Olmstead Properties signed Luckin Coffee to 10-year, 1,200-sq-ft retail lease at 180 Varick St., Hudson Square, NYC.
Luckin Coffee replaces 40-year-old pizzeria/deli; property owned by Rosenblatt family since 1920s development.
Luckin is one of fastest-growing coffee brands; Olmstead focusing on amenities to enhance tenant experience and community.
stories.summary: Olmstead Properties signed Luckin Coffee, a rapidly growing coffee brand, to a 10-year, 1,200-square-foot retail lease at 180 Varick Street in Hudson Square, replacing a multi-decade pizzeria and deli. The historic office building, developed in the 1920s, has been owned by the Rosenblatt family since inception and remains Olmstead's longest-held asset.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. Hudson Square office-to-retail tenant turnover and modernization reflect post-pandemic repositioning of office buildings with strong ground-floor retail. Rising urban coffee/QSR chains signal renewed daytime foot traffic and office population recovery in Manhattan; this is a positive indicator for residential fundamentals in walkable NYC submarkets with strong office anchors.

stories.title: Northmarq Arranges Refi for Grocery-Anchored Queens Retail
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s New York Metro Debt + Equity team led by Robert Delitsky and Keith Braddish arranged the $15-million refinance of Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center. The 34,949-square-foot, multi-tenant anchored center is located at 102-20 Atlantic Avenue in the Ozone Park section of Queens. Northmarq arranged the financing on behalf of the owner, Schuckman Realty Inc., through a relationship with a commercial bank. “We are thrilled to have arranged this financing for our long-time client on this premier retail center,” Delitsky said. “This transaction reflects the continued strength of well-located retail properties in the boroughs and Northmarq’s ability to deliver financing solutions to meet our clients’ objectives.” Added Ken Schuckman, president of Schuckman Realty, “Grocery-anchored retail in the boroughs is as strong as we’ve ever seen it — well-located neighborhood centers with daily-needs tenants are outperforming the market, and lenders know it.” Built in 1984, Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center is leased to daily-needs tenants including Bravo Supermarkets, Lenox Hill Radiology, Four Leaf Federal Credit Union and Dunkin’. bullets: Northmarq arranged $15M refi for Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center, Ozone Park, Queens; 34,949 sq ft, multi-tenant anchor.

stories.summary: Northmarq's New York Metro team arranged a $15M refinance for Atlantic Plaza Shopping Center, a 34,949-square-foot grocery-anchored retail property in Ozone Park, Queens. Built in 1984, the center is leased to daily-needs anchors (Bravo, Dunkin') and service tenants. The owner and lender acknowledged strong fundamentals in borough grocery-anchored retail.
stories.impact: Demonstrates lender confidence in essential-retail fundamentals in outer boroughs. Grocery anchors and daily-needs tenants in Queens and Brooklyn are resilient demand drivers. Multifamily developers should note that Queens neighborhoods with mature, anchored retail centers have established convenience infrastructure—a positive signal for residential demand and rent sustainability in those submarkets. Ozone Park's retail strength supports adjacent multifamily demand.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Closes $12.5M Sale of La Mesa Seniors Housing
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of 5035-49 Guava Ave., an 81-unit seniors affordable multifamily property located in La Mesa. The property sold for $12.5 million, or $154,320 per unit. “Age-restricted communities with long-term affordability protections are rarely available for acquisition in San Diego County,” said Christopher Zorbas, executive managing director investments. “This transaction reflects the continued demand for well-maintained affordable senior housing, and despite broader industry headwinds, we remain confident in the long-term fundamentals of the La Mesa and greater San Diego rental market.” said Graeme Henderson, director of investments. “New ownership is poised to keep providing low-income senior housing for years to come, given the property is the only senior deed restricted building with an agreement in perpetuity in the submarket.”  Zorbas, Henderson and Austin Huffman, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s San Diego Del Mar office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a private owner, and procured the buyer, Positive Investments, based out of Los Angeles. The sale marks one of five transactions over 80 units in La Mesa and one of seven senior affordable transactions countywide in the past five years. The marketing team conducted over 20 tours of the 1986-vintage asset and had multiple competing offers. The conversations behind tomorrow’s apartment deals happen at Connect Apartments on September 22 in LA. Connect with the capital sources, owners, developers, and brokers driving multifamily investment. Learn more and reserve your seat at www.connectapts2026.com. bullets: Marcus & Millichap closed $12.5M sale of 81-unit seniors affordable multifamily, 5035-49 Guava Ave., La Mesa, CA.

stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of an 81-unit, age-restricted affordable seniors multifamily property in La Mesa, California for $12.5M ($154,320 per unit) to Positive Investments. The property includes long-term affordability protections and is rare in San Diego County. This transaction reflects continued demand for well-maintained affordable senior housing despite broader headwinds.
stories.impact: Scarcity of age-restricted affordable seniors housing with long-term deed restrictions creates a specialized submarket. San Diego's demographic aging and limited supply of affordable seniors units support development feasibility, but regulatory burdens and rent caps compress returns. For developers, this signals opportunity in seniors-focused builds in supply-constrained California markets, but only with strong tax-credit or public-funding partnerships. La Mesa's activity (5 large transactions in 5 years) shows active investor interest in this micro-market.

stories.title: NAI DiLeo-Bram Markets Piscataway Industrial in Key Supply Chain Corridor
stories.excerpt: NAI DiLeo-Bram & Co. (NAIDB) is marketing 240 Circle Drive North, a 74,500-square-foot industrial building situated on approximately five acres in Piscataway, NJ. The property features a 6,000-square-foot office component and is suited for an owner-user buyer seeking to establish or expand their strategic foothold in this Central New Jersey supply chain corridor. The marketing assignment is being led by the NAIDB brokerage team of VPs Kyle Gerace and Chris Chiusolo alongside COO David A. Simon. The team has multi-decade familiarity with the property associated with Managing Director Chris Galiano’s involvement in past leasing transactions. Positioned within the Piscataway industrial hub, the property is easily accessible via two separate I-287 interchanges, which directly connect with the New Jersey Turnpike, Garden State Parkway, Routes 1, 18, 22, I-78 and I-80. “Opportunities of this size for user-buyers are exceedingly rare in today’s market, especially within land-constrained infill corridors,” said Gerace. “Based on the current market cycle, 240 Circle Drive North delivers the exact combination of heavy power, functional logistics infrastructure and strategic regional connectivity that modern operators require to insulate and scale their businesses.”  The post NAI DiLeo-Bram Markets Piscataway Industrial in Key Supply Chain Corridor appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NAI DiLeo-Bram marketing 240 Circle Drive North, Piscataway, NJ: 74,500 sq ft industrial, ~5 acres, 6,000 sq ft office.
Property positioned in Central NJ supply-chain corridor; dual I-287 access to NJ Turnpike, Garden State Parkway, Routes 1/18/22, I-78/I-80.
Broker note: large user-buy opportunities rare in land-constrained infill; seeking owner-users to establish/expand in corridor.
stories.summary: NAI DiLeo-Bram is marketing 240 Circle Drive North, a 74,500-square-foot industrial building on ~5 acres in Piscataway, New Jersey, with 6,000 square feet of office. The property sits in a critical Central Jersey supply-chain corridor with dual I-287 interchange access and direct connections to the NJ Turnpike, major routes, and highways. The team is targeting owner-user buyers seeking to establish or expand operations.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, Piscataway industrial demand reflects continued logistics/supply-chain hub growth in the Northeast Corridor. Strong industrial fundamentals and land constraints near major highways signal infrastructure bottlenecks. For multifamily developers, this suggests worker-population growth in Central NJ distribution centers and logistics hubs—translate to rental demand in nearby residential submarkets. Industrial employment concentration often precedes residential demand spikes in secondary markets.

stories.title: Peachtree Lends $113M on Apartments’ Conversion to Margaritaville Hotel Savannah
stories.excerpt: Tidal Real Estate Partners is “waving” hello to the opportunity to convert a Savannah, Ga., multifamily building into a Margaritaville-branded hotel. The New York City development firm just sealed $113 million of bridge debt to recapitalize and repurpose the 2023-built Ann Street Lofts property into the 230-key Margaritaville Hotel Savannah, Commercial Observer has learned. Peachtree Group originated the three-year floating-rate loan with two 12-month extension options for the multifamily-to-hospitality conversion project in Downtown Savannah. The conversion project is slated to commence late this summer. Jared Schlosser, head of credit originations at Peachtree Group, said after developing Ann Street Lofts as Georgia’s first large-scale mass timber multifamily project, Tidal opted to pivot the 232-unit property to hotel use after evaluating market conditions. Schlosser noted that the property is positioned for success given Savannah’s strong tourism numbers, with more than 18 million annual visitors coupled with a limited lodging supply within the city’s Historic District. “There’s a lot of development happening in this immediate area and a lot of planned development happening in this immediate area,” Schlosser told Commercial Observer. “The market continues to have a big influx of tourism and conferences so there is a good mix of demand drivers.” Walker & Dunlop negotiated the debt with a team led by Michael Brown and Keith Kurland. The Margaritaville Hotel Savannah is slated to debut in summer 2027. It will include a hotel pool deck, a Jimmy Buffett’s Margaritaville restaurant concept, and a LandShark Bar & Grill. Schlosser said the hotel will be designed for both leisure travelers as well as local residents seeking food, beverage and resort-style amenities. bullets: Peachtree Group funded $113M bridge debt for Tidal Real Estate's Ann Street Lofts (Savannah) conversion to 230-key Margaritaville Hotel.
Property: 232-unit mass-timber multifamily (2023), 3-year floating-rate bridge with two 12-month extensions; pivot to hospitality.

stories.summary: Tidal Real Estate Partners secured a $113M bridge loan from Peachtree Group to convert Ann Street Lofts, a 232-unit mass-timber multifamily property completed in 2023 in Downtown Savannah, into a 230-key Margaritaville-branded hotel. The floating-rate bridge has a three-year term with two 12-month extension options. Tidal opted to pivot from residential to hospitality after evaluating market conditions and Savannah's strong 18M+ annual visitor base.
stories.impact: Multifamily-to-hospitality conversion signals market-driven asset redeployment: soft residential fundamentals in Savannah (or poor multifamily underwriting at acquisition) made hospitality a higher-return alternative. This flags potential oversupply or demand softness in Savannah's multifamily market post-2023. Developers should scrutinize Savannah residential absorption and rent trends; strong tourism + hotel conversion could indicate tightening multifamily supply, but poor timing of multifamily delivery could also signal execution missteps. Watch comparable Sunbelt markets (Charleston, New Orleans) for similar conversions as a canary for residential market stress.
